question: Did clean water and sewers do more than better food to cut deaths in industrial cities?
answer: Clean water was the sharpest single blow to death. In major US cities from 1900 to 1936, filtration and chlorination explain nearly half the fall in total mortality, three-quarters of the fall in infant deaths and nearly two-thirds of the fall in child deaths. Cities that cleaned their water saw typhoid collapse within years.
move: Whichever side you took, the order in which deaths fell is what decides it.
counterpoint: Deaths were falling before the pipes arrived. In England and Wales, tuberculosis, spread through the air, killed fewer people decade after decade from the mid-1800s, long before any drug or sewer could touch it; better-fed bodies resisted it. And a re-analysis of the same US cities found filtration explained much less of the decline.
reference: Cutler & Miller, The Role of Public Health Improvements in Health Advances: The Twentieth-Century United States, Demography, 2005
